newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo tobacco plant DIV stifled by illegal trade.
newsitem.headline: Yugo tobacco plant DIV stifled by illegal trade.

text.p: The tobacco factory Duvanska Industrija Vranje (DIV) could face bankruptcy unless cigarette smuggling is halted soon, DIV sources said on Monday.

"Unless illegal trade is stopped soon, in a few months we will have to halt production because we are struggling with huge stocks of around 300 tonnes of cigarettes," DIV general manager Slavoljub Vuckovic told Reuters.
DIV, which has a capacity of around 350 tonnes of cigarettes per month, produced less than 60 tonnes and sold only 46 tonnes in 1997. One tonne is equivalent to about 50,000 packs.
"With such thin sales, it will take five to six months just to sell existing stocks," Vuckovic said.
DIV last year produced 1,100 tonnes of cigarettes, less than a third of its annual production before the breakup of former Yugoslavia in 1991.

The Serbian government introduced tax stamps on cigarettes and alcoholic drinks last summer in an effort to curb smuggling which became widespread during a 3-1/2 year trade embargo against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro.
But local producers said the move has had little effect other than to raise their prices, making their products even less competitive against much cheaper contraband.
Foreign cigarettes sold in the streets are mainly smuggled in from Bulgaria, Macedonia and Albania, with Marlboro, Lucky Strike, LM, Bond, Lord, Dunhill and Rothmans among the most popular brands.
Street prices range from five dinars (92 cents) (Bond, LM) to 12 dinars (Davidoff) per pack and are on average 30 to 50 percent cheaper than those sold legally.
Although cheaper, local cigarettes are less popular.
The Tobacco Fund earlier this month said Serbia lost around 1.26 billion dinars ($230 million) in uncollected 1996 tax revenues due to the illegal cigarette trade.
According to the fund's figures, domestic producers sold slightly over 7,000 tonnes of cigarettes in 1996, or less than 30 percent of estimated annual consumption of 23,000 tonnes.
In an economy devastated by the breakup of the former Yugoslav federation and international sanctions, hundreds of thousands of people turned to the black market for a livelihood.
Vuckovic said it was not clear why the government has not taken more stringent measures to curb the grey economy despite frequent pledges.
"Those are not insignificant quantities we are talking about. That is something only the state and customs administration can stop," he said. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
